newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Chechnya's new leader faces tough tasks.
newsitem.headline: Chechnya's new leader faces tough tasks.

text.p: Chechen rebel Shamil Basayev, Russia's most wanted "terrorist", conceded defeat on Wednesday to his rival Aslan Maskhadov in the election for president of the breakaway republic.

Maskhadov, commander of Chechen fighters in their victorious war against the Russian army, defeated Basayev, his closest challenger, by a runaway margin of three to one, according to preliminary results from Monday's polls.

Electoral Commission head Mumadi Saydaiyev told a news conference that Maskhadov, 46, whose rebel army forced Russian troops out of Chechnya last year, won 64.8 percent of the vote -- more than all other candidates taken together.
He said prominent field commander Basayev, 32, was second with 22.7 percent and acting Chechen president Zelimkhan Yandarbiyev was third on 10.2 percent, with votes counted in 56 districts out of 63.

International observers strongly praised the election on Wednesday. "What we saw was democracy against a backdrop of ruins," said Poland's Tadeusz Iwinski, vice-president of the Council of Europe's observer team.

Ivan Rybkin, secretary of Russia's policy-making Security Council, hailed the poll as a further step towards peace and stability in the turbulent Caucasian region and told reporters Russia was ready to resume negotiations.

But former Soviet army colonel Maskhadov, despite his landslide victory and his cautious welcome by Russia, may find it difficult to meet his campaign vows to restore stability and crown struggle for independence with international recognition.
Yandarbiyev and Basayev, contradicting their own pre-election promises, made clear they were not planning to cooperate with Maskhadov.
Yandarbiyev told Russian television that he did not see any place for him in Maskhadov's future administration and that he generally distrusted his rival's entourage.
Basayev, who led a bloody hostage-taking raid on the Russian town of Budennovsk in 1995 in which more than 100 people were killed, announced he would quit politics for the computer business.
But he added that he would not actively oppose Maskhadov. "I won't get in his way," Basayev said at his headquarters in the devastated Minutka area of the Chechen capital Grozny.
"I will get on with my own private life. I will get on with business, the computer business," he added.

Maverick field commander Salman Raduyev, whose fighters carried out a hostage raid in January 1996 in neighbouring ethnic region of Dagestan, said he did not recognise the polls and was planning new terror attacks on Russia.
"At least three Russian cities must be burned to cinders," Raduyev, told Reuters in his village in eastern Chechnya. "We are working on a major operation codenamed 'Ash'."
Raduyev believes that Chechen leader Dzhokhar Dudayev, reported killed in a Russian rocket attack last year, is still alive and has refused to obey any other leader.
Maskhadov promised on Tuesday to reopen talks with Russia on recognition of Chechen sovereignty and launch a campaign to win international recognition for the breakaway southern province.
But he insisted that this should be done through political means.
Interfax news agency quoted a source in the Russian government as saying that Moscow was ready to resume talks immdiately after inauguration of the new Chechen leader.
Itar-Tass news agency quoted a senior Chechen official as saying that the inauguration ceremony could take place within two months after the official announcement of election results.

Moscow and rebels struck a peace deal in August under which Russia withdrew its forces sent in late 1994 to quell Chechnya's independence bid and the separatist leaders agreed to defer by five years the decision on the region's political status.

President Boris Yeltsin's press secretary said on Tuesday that the Kremlin leader, recovering from pneumonia, had cautiously welcomed Maskhadov's success but made clear that Moscow still rejected full independence for Chechnya.

In another upset to Maskhadov the envoy of the Organisation of Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) said that the polls, which OSCE observers found free and fair, gave no new arguments to pro-independence campaigners.

"From the point of view of the international community Chechnya remains part of the Russian Federation," the head of the OSCE mission in Chechnya Tim Guldimann told Russian television. "The election changed nothing about this."
But for all the stunning success of Maskhadov's military and electoral campaigns, the political and economic task facing him is a daunting one and Russia still holds many strong cards.
Maskhadov himself admitted on Tuesday: "Our economic situation is woeful...nearly everything has been destroyed."
The silver-haired commander demanded reparations from Russia and said he plans to negotiate a share of revenues from lucrative Russian oil pipelines that cross Chechen territory.
Moscow has promised reconstruction aid and has offered a share of oil profits to tempt the Chechens out of seceding.
